# Angular Phase 0 - Screen/Route Inventory & Risk Classification

*Generated by `tools/angular-audit/run_audit.py`, a static-analysis pass over the live AngularJS 1.5 routing configuration. Read-only — no application code was touched to produce this document. This is Phase 0 of the frontend rebuild plan: a full inventory and a first-pass risk tag on every screen, so later phases can be sequenced by risk instead of by convenience.*

**How this document was built, in plain terms:** the AngularJS app defines every screen as a "state" (a URL + a view template + a controller) in one central routing file. Instead of reading all of those definitions by hand — which would be slow and inconsistent — this was done with a small, reusable tool suite (`tools/angular-audit/`) that parses the actual routing file and cross-references it against the real view and controller files on disk. Risk tags (clinical-safety / billing) were then applied by scanning each screen's name, URL, and file path for a curated list of keywords (e.g. "transfusion", "dose", "invoice", "tariff"), plus a per-module default for departments that are clinical or billing by nature (e.g. everything under Blood Bank defaults to clinical-safety-relevant even if the individual screen name doesn't contain an obvious keyword).

**This is a first-pass heuristic sort, not a clinical or billing sign-off.** It exists to separate the ~345 screens that are most likely safe to rebuild quickly from the ~1204 that touch money, patient safety, or both, so the right expert reviews the right screens later (Phase 6). Treat every "yes" and "unclear" tag below as a starting point for that expert review, not a final verdict — and treat every "no" as provisional too: keyword/module matching can miss things a human reader would catch. Where the tooling genuinely couldn't tell (missing files, unresolvable controllers, states with no view), that is called out explicitly below rather than guessed at.

---

## Headline numbers

- **Total screens/routes found: 1567** — 1098 from `resources/assets/js/config/app.js` (the app's central `$stateProvider` configuration) plus **469 more from 469 other files that self-register their own state(s) from their own `.config($stateProvider)` block**, outside app.js entirely. This second category was missed by the original version of this scan (corrected 2026-07-18 — see `docs/ANGULAR_PENDING_FINDINGS.md` entry 3 for how the gap was found). Only live, currently-loaded code counts toward either number: commented-out state definitions are excluded, and so are states defined by a file whose own `<script>` tag in `index.html` is commented out or absent (`tools/angular-audit/data/dead_states.json` lists those separately, for anyone who wants to see what was deliberately excluded rather than silently dropped).
- **56 modules/departments** identified from the view-template folder structure.
- **Risk tiers:**
  - Both clinical-safety AND billing relevant: **81** (5%)
  - Clinical-safety relevant only: **521** (33%)
  - Billing relevant only: **602** (38%)
  - Low risk (neither, by this pass): **345** (22%)
  - Unclear / needs runtime verification: **18** (1%)

**In plain terms: 1204 out of 1567 screens (roughly 76%) touch either patient safety or money in some way.** Only 345 screens (about 22%) look administrative/low-risk on this first pass.

## Known gaps and things that need runtime verification, not guessing

- **5 states reference a controller name that could not be matched to any controller file on disk** by static registration-pattern search (e.g. component-style controllers, unconventional naming, or possibly dead/unused states). Listed individually in the appendix below. These need someone to load the actual screen and confirm what controller (if any) really runs.
- **3 states have no resolvable `templateUrl`** (they use a multi-view `views: {...}` block instead of a single template, which this pass did not expand). Listed below.
- **13 states point at a `templateUrl` that does not exist on disk** at the expected path — likely dead routes, renamed files, or a build-time template pipeline this pass didn't account for. Listed below.
- **372 states share one of a small number of generic, reused controllers** (the largest being a single shared `common-controller.js` used by 353 different screens as `MasterController`). **Corrected 2026-07-17, during the Phase 2 pilot audit** (`docs/PHASE2_PILOT_AUDIT.md`): this doc originally hypothesized `MasterController` "likely branches internally on the current state/URL" — read in full during the pilot audit, it does not. It has no `$state.current.name`/URL check anywhere; it's a flat generic scope-initializer (shared tab state, date-picker flags, and a `customEvent` listener that maps ~35 known master-screen names to sidebar title text) that every one of the 353 screens gets identically regardless of which one is active. The real per-screen behavior lives entirely in each screen's own view template — which of `MasterController`'s generic scope properties it happens to bind to, and, per the pilot audit's `homecareMedicationApproval` finding, possibly nothing at all if the view was never wired to a backend call. For these states, the "API calls" and "cross-screen coupling" columns in the table below still reflect the *entire shared controller file*, not the specific screen — determining what a given shared-controller screen actually does still requires reading that screen's own view template or a runtime trace, just not for the reason originally guessed here. See `tools/golden-trace/`, built for exactly this.
- **Form field counts** are a raw count of `<input>`, `<select>`, and `<textarea>` tags in the view's HTML file. This over-counts on views that conditionally show/hide fields with `ng-if`/`ng-show` and under-counts any field injected dynamically by the controller rather than written directly in the template. Treat it as a rough complexity signal, not an exact form-field census.
- **Risk tags are keyword/module-heuristic, not a reading of each screen's actual clinical or billing logic.** This is exactly the kind of judgment call Phase 6 assigns to a real clinician/billing reviewer, not to this automated pass.
- **Bed management and appointment-scheduling screens were tagged administrative (low-risk) by default in this pass**, but bed placement can carry real infection-control/isolation implications in some hospitals. Worth a specific yes/no from a clinical lead before treating those 10 bed-management screens as safe to rebuild casually.
- **`accessControlController` (the controller behind the `accessControl`/`accessControl1` states) is registered twice, in two different files — resolved 2026-07-17, `access-control.js` wins.** `index.html` loads `resources/assets/accessControl/controller/accessControlController.js` at line 1778 (60 lines, a minimal stub — just a `remove` scope function) and then `resources/assets/js/controller/access-control/access-control.js` at line 1786 (373 lines, the full implementation — `$state`/`$cookies`/`GenericService`/`BillingGenericService`/`ivhTreeview*` injected, sets `$scope.title = "Access Control"`). AngularJS's `.controller()` registration silently overwrites same-named entries with no error, so whichever loads *last* wins — **`access-control.js` (373 lines) is the one that actually runs; the 60-line stub is dead code, silently shadowed on every page load.** If Phase 2+ ever characterizes an access-control screen, `access-control.js` is the behavior to capture/rebuild — the other file can be deleted separately as a follow-up cleanup, but that's an application-code change outside this doc's read-only scope. Both are still excluded from the API-call/coupling columns above (this bullet documents the fact directly instead).
- **Four files under the Nursing/pharmacy controller path are unresolved git-merge-tool conflict artifacts** (`addNewbillableConsumptionController_REMOTE_6240.js`, `_BASE_6240.js`, `_BACKUP_6240.js`, `_LOCAL_6240.js`, sitting alongside the real `addNewbillableConsumptionController.js`) — leftover debris from a past merge conflict, excluded from this scan. Worth a separate, low-priority cleanup pass.

## Methodology detail

**Route extraction:** every `.state('name', { ... })` call in `app.js` **and** in any other `.js` file under the whole webapp tree that self-registers its own state(s) from its own `.config($stateProvider)` block is parsed with a balanced-paren scanner (not a regex-only pass, to correctly handle nested objects like `resolve` blocks). Commented-out state definitions are stripped first and excluded, as are `.state()`-shaped calls belonging to unrelated bundled libraries (jQuery UI, Kendo UI both have their own, unrelated `.state()` widget methods — filtered both by known vendor file path and, as a second line of defense, by requiring a resolvable literal string state name). A state registered by a file outside `app.js` only counts as live if that file's own `<script>` tag in `index.html` is actually present and not commented out — cross-referenced directly against `index.html`, not assumed. See `tools/angular-audit/extract_states.py`.

**Module classification:** derived entirely from the view template's folder path, cross-checked against the actual `views/` directory tree on disk. See `classify_risk.py::classify_module`.

**Controller resolution:** every `.js` file under the whole `webapp/` tree (vendor libraries and known dead git-merge-artifact files excluded) is scanned for its actual `.controller('Name', [...])` registration, handling multi-line registrations and controller names containing a literal `.`. See `build_controller_index.py`.

**API-call complexity:** counted as calls to the app's shared HTTP service wrappers (`GenericService.*`, `BillingGenericService.*`, `GenericServiceParamHeader.*`) or raw `$http.get/post/put/delete` inside the resolved controller file. States sharing a heavily-reused generic controller (≥4 states) are marked "shared" and show the aggregate count for that shared file instead — not meaningfully per-screen.

**Cross-screen coupling:** each resolved controller file is scanned for `$rootScope.$broadcast(...)`, `$scope.$on(...)`/`$rootScope.$on(...)`, and direct `$rootScope.xxx = ...` writes.
